advisor.summary: A defined benefit plan promises a future benefit — up to a $290,000 annual life annuity at 2026 limits under §415(b) — and deducts whatever the actuary certifies is needed to fund the promise under §404(o). Because the constraint is a benefit rather than a contribution cap, an owner in their fifties with high, stable income routinely supports $150,000–$300,000 of annual deductions — multiples of the $72,000 defined-contribution world. The cash balance variant states the promise as a hypothetical account (pay credit plus interest credit), which is easier to communicate and to divide among partners. The admission price is commitment: minimum funding is mandatory every year under §§412, 430, and the plan needs an enrolled actuary, a TPA, and a multi-year horizon. The engine applies whatever contribution is entered, capped at owner compensation — the real number must come from the actuarial valuation each year, and it will drift.
mechanics: The actuary works backward from the promised benefit — capped at a $290,000-per-year annuity under §415(b) for 2026 — to a required annual contribution; fewer years to retirement means a larger required amount, which is why the design structurally favors owners roughly 45 to 62.
The deduction follows the actuarial funding target under §404(o) rather than a percent-of-compensation cap — the mechanism that lets funding run to multiples of any defined-contribution limit.
Minimum funding under §§412, 430 is compulsory each year once the plan is adopted; the benefit formula must be set at a level the business can sustain through a weak year.

Compensation counts only up to the §401(a)(17) cap ($360,000 for 2026), and the benefit formula needs W-2 wages or self-employment earnings large enough to support it — for S corporation owners this is a reasonable-compensation conversation before it is a plan-design conversation.

In cash balance form each participant receives a stated pay credit plus an interest credit — legally a defined benefit plan, visually an account, and far easier to explain and to split among partners.

For a self-employed owner the deduction is above-the-line and reduces the §199A QBI base — often deliberately, since it can pull income back under the QBI phase-out; the engine models the contribution the same way, capped at earned income.

authority.note: The maximum annual benefit — $290,000 for 2026 — that the actuary funds toward.
The deduction limit for defined benefit plans tracks the actuarially determined funding target — the statutory engine of the six-figure deduction.
Minimum funding standards: the contribution is mandatory every year the plan exists.
Caps compensation counted in the benefit formula at $360,000 for 2026.
Owner-side plan deductions reduce qualified business income; near the phase-out the interaction can add to — or subtract from — the modeled benefit.
The permanency requirement — a plan funded briefly and then frozen or terminated risks disqualification.
2026 COLA figures for the §415(b) and §401(a)(17) limits relied on in this record.

requirements: High, stable income sufficient to sustain the certified contribution for several consecutive years — a commitment, not an annual election.
An enrolled actuary and TPA engagement covering the design study, annual valuation, and Schedule SB certification.
Owner age generally 45 or older for the math to dominate defined-contribution alternatives, with W-2 or self-employment compensation that supports the benefit formula.
If employees exist: a census-priced design study first, because nondiscrimination testing will require meaningful staff benefits.
risks: The leading challenge theory is permanency: a plan funded hard for a year or two and then frozen or terminated invites disqualification arguments under Reg. §1.401-1(b)(2) — set the benefit at a level sustainable across the commitment period, typically three to five years or more.
Funding is mandatory in down years; a missed minimum contribution triggers §4971 excise taxes and a funding-deficiency spiral.
Investment risk stays with the employer: returns above the assumption overfund the plan, while poor returns raise the required contribution.
Ongoing costs — actuary, TPA, Form 5500/Schedule SB, and PBGC premiums when staff are covered — typically run $2,000–$5,000+ per year against the deduction.
Distributions are ordinary income later: this is deferral plus bracket arbitrage, not permanent exclusion, and the endgame (terminate near retirement and roll to an IRA) needs its own plan.
stateNotes: States that conform to federal AGI or federal taxable income allow the deduction in full with no addback — verify conformity in separate-computation states in the client's footprint.
PTET interaction: when the entity funds the plan, the deduction shrinks the pass-through income base a PTET election is computed on — re-project PTET estimates after the funding decision.
Missouri conforms through RSMo §143.121; for Missouri SALT Parity Act PTET electors (RSMo §143.436), fourth-quarter PTET estimates should reflect the certified contribution.
reviewChecklist: Actuarial design study is in the file and the modeled contribution equals the certified number, not an aspiration.
Multi-year cash-flow stress test done — the client can fund the minimum in a weak year without borrowing.
Owner compensation supports the benefit formula and passes reasonable-compensation review (S corporation owners).
Census reviewed and staff cost priced where employees exist; the conflicting cash-balance-stack strategy is not also selected.
Adoption and funding deadlines calendared: document by the filing deadline, funding no later than 8½ months after year-end.
QBI phase-out interplay reviewed so the modeled benefit reflects the client's real marginal picture.

client.teaser: A pension for your own business — with deductions far past normal plan limits.
client.headline: The six-figure deduction built for owners closer to retirement
plainEnglish: Remember pensions? They promised workers a set monthly check for life. Big firms mostly dropped them. But the law still allows them, and you can set one up for your own business.

Here is why that matters. Normal retirement accounts cap what goes in each year. A pension works backward from the benefit you are promised at retirement. The closer you are to that date, the more you may put in now — and every dollar is deductible. For an owner in their fifties with strong income, that often means $150,000 or more per year.
The trade-off is commitment. A specialist sets the amount, and you must fund it every year, for several years. So we only recommend it when your income is strong and steady.
client.analogy: Filling a bucket by age 65 from age 30 takes only a slow drip. Starting at 55, you are allowed to pour much faster — and deduct every gallon.
benefits: Deductions of $150,000 to $300,000 a year are common for older owners
The older you are, the more you can put away
Builds a large retirement fund in a short span of years
Can pair with a 401(k) layer for even more (we model that separately)
steps: WE commission a design study with a pension specialist to find your exact number.
WE stress-test your cash flow so the required funding fits even a slow year.
WE set up the plan and calendar every funding and filing deadline.
YOU fund the certified amount each year and send the specialist your payroll data.
clientCommitments: Fund the required amount every year — it is not optional once the plan exists
Keep the plan in place for several years; quick exits cause problems
Get us the census and payroll data the actuary needs each year
